name: Apache Zeppelin
summary: A self-hosted web notebook where each paragraph runs through an interpreter: Spark, Flink, JDBC, Python and more. Maintained, but behind Jupyter and Databricks in reach.
intro: A Zeppelin server is a Java web application: you open notes in the browser, and each note is a list of paragraphs that start with an interpreter name such as `%spark.sql`, `%flink`, `%jdbc` or `%python`. The server doesn’t run your code itself. Each interpreter group (for example Spark, which bundles Scala, PySpark, IPySpark, SparkR and Spark SQL) runs in its own JVM process and talks to the server over Thrift; binding modes decide whether all users share one interpreter process or get one per user or per note. Results come back as text, HTML or tables that the notebook draws as charts without extra code, and notes can run on a built-in cron schedule or be created and run through a REST API.

Zeppelin is free under Apache 2.0 and you host it yourself; the official image is `apache/zeppelin`. It is not retired: 0.12.0 (January 2025) introduced a new UI, 0.12.1 followed in June 2026, and commits land almost daily. But the project reports only moderate activity, its interpreters trail the engines (support for Spark 4.1 and 4.2 is still an open ticket), and JDK 17 support is planned for 0.13.0. In the cloud it lives on mostly inside other products: Amazon EMR installs Zeppelin 0.11.1, and Studio notebooks in Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink are powered by it.
strengths: One notebook mixes engines: a Spark SQL paragraph, a Flink streaming query and a JDBC query against PostgreSQL can sit side by side
Built-in charts and dynamic forms turn SQL results into simple dashboards without writing plotting code
Interpreters run in separate processes per user or per note, with Shiro authentication and note permissions for shared servers
Can also run Jupyter kernels through its Jupyter interpreter, and exposes a REST API for creating and running notes
limits: Insecure by default: anonymous access is allowed until you configure Shiro, and the April 2026 board report mentions outstanding security issues under investigation
Interpreters lag their engines: Spark 4.1 and 4.2 support is still open, the Flink interpreter needs Flink 1.15 or later, and JDK 17 support is planned for 0.13.0
Outside the Spark and Flink niche, Jupyter is the broader tool: its kernels cover dozens of languages, which Zeppelin itself reaches only by bridging to Jupyter kernels
Mostly self-run: you deploy, upgrade and secure the server and each interpreter; AWS embeds it in EMR and Managed Service for Apache Flink, at older versions (EMR 7.14 ships 0.11.1)
Several interpreters were removed in 0.11 (Beam, Scio, ksqlDB, Kotlin, Lens), so old notes can stop working after an upgrade

sections.title: Zeppelin, Jupyter or Databricks notebooks?
sections.intro: All three put code, results and notes in one page. They differ in who runs them and how many languages and engines one notebook can mix.

rows.label: Licence and hosting
values: Proprietary, part of the Databricks platform

rows.label: Languages
values: Per paragraph, through interpreters: Spark (Scala, Python, R, SQL), Flink, JDBC, Python and more
One kernel per notebook; kernels exist for dozens of languages

rows.label: Where code runs
values: Interpreter processes next to the server, or on Spark and Flink clusters
A kernel process per notebook (IPython by default), on a laptop or a server

rows.label: Many users
values: One server with Shiro login and note permissions
JupyterHub gives each user their own server

rows.label: Charts
values: Through plotting libraries in the kernel

notes: Pick Zeppelin for a self-hosted notebook that mixes Spark, Flink and SQL in one page, or when EMR or Managed Flink already provide one. Pick Jupyter for one-language notebooks, especially Python, and use Databricks notebooks if your data and compute are on Databricks.

story: By 2013 teams had several SQL engines over Hadoop, such as Hive, Presto and Shark, but no friendly open-source tool to explore data with them and see the results as charts. Zeppelin began at NFLabs in Korea as a GUI for those SQL-over-Hadoop systems, open source from its start in September 2013; Lee Moon Soo was among its core developers.

It soon became clear that data scientists wanted more than SQL: a web notebook where they could share interactive sessions on a cluster. Zeppelin added full Apache Spark support and a collaborative, notebook-style interface with pluggable interpreters for other systems. Developers from NFLabs and Between proposed it to Apache, and it entered the Incubator in December 2014.
Zeppelin became a top-level Apache project in May 2016. It found its niche where Spark, Flink and SQL meet: Amazon EMR ships it, and AWS built its Flink Studio notebooks on it.

choices.choice: Pluggable interpreters instead of one language
choices.why: Zeppelin started as a front end for several SQL-on-Hadoop engines. An abstract interpreter API let it add Spark, Flink and JDBC sources without changing the notebook.

Each engine needs its own libraries and resources. Running each interpreter group in its own JVM, talking to the server over Thrift, keeps engines apart from the web server and lets one setting serve shared, per-user or per-note sessions.
The goal was data exploration and visualization for analysts. Rendering SQL results as tables and charts by default saved writing plotting code for every query.
